opinions.name: Richardson v. Thunder, LLC
opinions.synopsis: Guests injured or killed in a multi-shooter shooting at an annual fraternity homecoming block party sued the national fraternity and the limited liability company that owned the house, asserting premises liability, negligence, and nuisance. Applying the Carmichael totality-of-the-circumstances framework, the Court of Appeals held that evidence of occasional fistfights at parties four or more years earlier and three police responses for crowd control or disorderly conduct, none involving weapons, injuries, or arrests, was not substantially similar to a multiparty shootout and did not create a jury issue on reasonable foreseeability. The court also found no other totality factors, such as a high-crime location, weapons previously observed at the parties, or a volatile situation brewing that night, and rejected the contention that a large party with alcohol is itself enough, noting that would make the proprietor an insurer of guest safety. Because no duty to guard against the criminal act arose, summary judgment was proper for both the fraternity and the property owner, and the derivative vicarious-liability claim failed for want of an underlying tort; the court noted the 2025 negligent security statutes, O.C.G.A. sections 51-3-50 through 51-3-57, do not apply to causes of action arising before April 21, 2025. Affirmed.
opinions.why: The decision applies the Carmichael foreseeability analysis to hold that generalized prior fights and crowd-control police calls are not substantially similar to a mass shooting, and confirms that the invitee/licensee distinction is largely irrelevant to third-party criminal conduct claims while the 2025 negligent security statutes do not reach earlier-arising claims.

opinions.name: Giles v. Greenhouse Apartments, LLC
opinions.synopsis: The Court of Appeals affirmed summary judgment for an apartment owner and its manager in a negligent-security action by a tenant beaten by unknown assailants on the property in 2020. The landlord conceded it owed the tenant a duty of ordinary care; the affirmance rests solely on causation — the tenant could not establish that any claimed security failure proximately caused the attack — and, given that holding, the court expressly declined to reach the equal-or-superior-knowledge and assumption-of-risk defenses and the challenge to excluded evidence of other crime in the area.
opinions.why: Causation is an independently dispositive element of a negligent-security claim: a defendant can win summary judgment without litigating foreseeability at all. The incident predates SB 68, so the common-law framework applies; for incidents on or after April 21, 2025 the analysis runs through the statutory regime at O.C.G.A. §§ 51-3-50 to 51-3-57.

opinions.name: Venetian Hills Apartments, LLC v. Hughes
opinions.synopsis: In a wrongful-death action after a tenant died in a fire set during an assault by another tenant's guest, the Court of Appeals held the landlord was not entitled to judgment notwithstanding the verdict: it could be liable under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-14 for defective construction and missing fire-safety measures even after parting with possession, and the criminal acts did not demand a defense verdict. The court nonetheless vacated the judgment and ordered a full retrial because the jury charges conflated landlord-tenant and premises-liability law.
opinions.why: A landlord can remain liable under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-14 for defective construction and missing fire-safety measures even after giving up possession, but jury charges that blend § 44-7-14 with § 51-3-1 premises law can require a full retrial.

opinions.name: Martin v. Six Flags Over Georgia II, L.P.
opinions.disposition: affirmed in part and reversed in part, and case remanded with direction
opinions.synopsis: The Supreme Court of Georgia held that a premises owner can be liable under OCGA section 51-3-1 for a criminal attack that begins on its premises but is completed off-premises, when the injuries are a foreseeable proximate result of the owner's breach of its duty to keep the premises safe, expressly adopting the principle from Wilks v. Piggly Wiggly Southern. The court clarified that the bus stop where the attack concluded was not part of the park's 'approaches,' because the owner had not exercised the control and dominion required to extend its duty to that public way. On apportionment, the court held that an apportionment error under OCGA section 51-12-33 ordinarily requires a retrial limited to the apportionment of fault among tortfeasors, not a full retrial, because the allocation of relative fault is a step distinct from the determinations of liability and total damages. The court affirmed liability, reversed the Court of Appeals' order of a full retrial, and remanded for retrial limited to apportionment.
opinions.why: The decision establishes that off-premises injuries can support landowner liability where the attack originates on the premises and is foreseeable, clarifies the 'approaches' and control-and-dominion analysis, and holds that apportionment error generally requires retrial only on apportionment rather than a full retrial.
